name: Invitation accepted
description: Tells the person who sent an invitation that it worked: who joined, what they can reach, what to do with them, and which invitations are still outstanding.

origin.note: Design: roster — a narrow measure, the new member as three ruled facts, boxed counts, and the invitations still outstanding kept as a closing ledger.

subject: {{ member_name }} joined {{ workspace_name }}
preheader: What they can already reach, and which invitations are still outstanding.

eyebrow.description: Small label above the headline, so a workspace owner who gets several of these a week can classify them at a glance.

member_name.description: Who accepted, by name. It leads the subject line because that is the only fact the recipient needs from the inbox list.

workspace_name.description: Which workspace they joined. Anyone who administers more than one needs this in the subject line to know which inbox rule applies.

intro.description: One sentence saying that access is already live, so the reader does not go looking for an approval step that does not exist.
intro.example: They accepted the invitation you sent on 14 September, and their access is already active.

joined_at.description: When they accepted. Useful mostly when it is much later than the invitation, which is the case worth noticing.

role_name.description: The role they came in on. Shown so the sender can catch a wrong role on the day it is granted rather than at the next access review.

member_email.description: The address they accepted with, set in the mono face. It is often not the address the invitation was sent to, and that difference is worth seeing.

member_count.description: How many people are now in the workspace, counting the new arrival.

members_caption.description: A short line under the member count — who is included in it, or what changed. It also keeps the two boxed figures the same height, which an unbalanced pair does not.

seats_value.description: Seats still available on the plan. Leave empty on plans that do not meter seats rather than showing an unbounded figure.

seats_caption.description: The consequence of running out, stated once and quietly. This is the only commercial line in the email and it should stay that way.
seats_caption.example: The next person added moves the plan to the next tier

next_heading.default: Worth doing while they are new

next_text.description: What the sender should actually do now. Without this the email is an announcement nobody acts on — a new member with nothing assigned is the most common way an invitation still fails.
next_text.example: New members are most likely to stay active if they have something of their own in the first week. Assign them a campaign, or point them at the one you invited them for.

primary_url.description: Where the sender goes to give the new member work, rather than a generic dashboard link.

secondary_label.description: Label for the lighter second action.

secondary_url.description: A second, lighter action — usually the permissions screen. Leave empty and the email carries one action instead of two.

pending_heading.description: Heading over the closing ledger of unaccepted invitations.

pending.description: Invitations sent and not yet accepted, as `text` (the address) and `detail` (how long it has been waiting, and when it expires). This is the part that gets a stalled rollout finished.

example.detail: Invited 4 days ago, expires on 21 September

closing.description: The closing line. Say who gets these emails, because the answer is usually 'every owner' and that is worth knowing before someone replies to all of them.
closing.default: Every workspace owner gets this email. Only owners can see the addresses listed above.
